items.note: No cooldown time to 10 K is stated in the University of Bremen MAPEX instrument entry (snapshot ae36fdc8904d8123), and no ZwickRoell or Bremen document giving a cooldown time for the HB 100 continuous-flow helium cryostat was found.

items.quote: The total net cool down time was approximately 26 days
items.document_title: D'Addabbo et al., The CUORE cryostat (J. Low Temp. Phys., arXiv:1805.06209)
items.note: Measured cooldown of the CUORE cryostat with the detector installed, ending at about 6.9 mK base temperature: about 22 days to 3.4 K, then 4 days of dilution-unit operation. The figure is net time. It leaves out a pause of about one month for exchange-gas pumping between the two phases. arXiv:2108.07883 reports the same run as 20 days before the dilution unit was switched on plus less than 4 days to reach 8 mK.
The NASA report on the custom Janis/DRS BIB-detector liquid-helium dewar (snapshot 11e2495bb43a5d88) gives no cooldown or precool time. No Janis document for this custom dewar was found.

items.value_as_printed: three days (install and cool down the sample)
items.quote: In our facility, it takes three days to install and cool down the sample and another three to warm up and remove it again.
items.document_title: ITER Newsline, Evaluating the ITER magnets at SULTAN
items.location: Interview text, paragraph on sample turnaround
items.note: A SULTAN operator statement. The 3 days covers installing and cooling down a conductor sample. The facility's background-field magnets stay cold, so this is an upper bound on sample cooldown. CAUTION: the source writes the number as a word ('three'), so a numeral check on the quote will fail. The only other source found, an IAEA FEC poster (snapshot 615b398e41f7ba92), also uses a word: a full warm-up plus cool-down thermal cycle 'lasts about four days'. No source gives the number as a numeral.

items.quote: Measurements at VTS1 revealed that total cool- down time is about 180 minutes
items.document_title: Shielding Studies for Superconducting RF Cavities at Fermilab (SATIF-10, arXiv:1202.1533)
items.location: VTS description (cavities tested in 2 K superfluid helium bath)
items.note: Measured at VTS1. The same paper gives only an estimate of about 240 minutes for VTS2 and VTS3, so that figure is not used. The experiment paper (arXiv:2307.10433) says 'VTS' without naming the stand. If the 2.6 GHz test ran in VTS2 or VTS3, this VTS1 value may not apply. The quote keeps the source's line-break hyphen ('cool- down').

The ITER articles 'Let there be cold' (snapshots 8a7ea77a6755d0ca / 896afca9901900ca) and 'Ready to enter commissioning' (09fed8c7fb7fd42b) give the date the pump reached about 5 K but not how long the cooldown took. A third-party summary describes cold testing as a 2 to 3 month procedure, but that is the whole campaign, not the cooldown.

items.quote: The first ITER coil was cooled to 4 K (minus 269 °C) over a 12-day period.
items.document_title: ITER, World's largest superconducting magnet test facility now operational (21 May 2026)
items.location: Press release, paragraph on first coil cooldown
items.note: The measured cooldown of the first 330-tonne toroidal field coil to 4 K, which is the configuration's first-coil 4 K point.

items.quote: The cryostat takes approximately 24 hours to cool down or heat up to room temperature relative to an
items.document_title: Bowens et al., The Michigan Infrared Test Thermal ELT N-band (MITTEN) Cryostat (Proc. SPIE 11447, 2020)
items.location: Section 4, Performance to date and future plans
items.note: The cooldown time to the 16 K optical-bench operating temperature, reported for this exact apparatus. The sentence goes on: 'ambient temperature of 16 K for the optical bench'.

The calorimeter has cryocoolers, so it does have a cooldown. None of these NASA Glenn sources states a cooldown time: the abstract (7d57e8d5e4c35347), the slides (0d9469ff4e4ba529), the design paper NTRS 20170000942 (6222ea7d853b2625) or the seam-test slides NTRS 20170008804 (86b3004b865d9251). The design paper mentions only 48 hours for the first 10 data points, which is test time.

items.document_title: Yang et al., Thermal Model Performance for the James Webb Space Telescope OTIS Cryo-Vacuum Test (ICES 2018-35, NASA GSFC slides, NTRS 20180004589)
items.location: Slide 10, As-Tested Full OTIS CV Profile
items.note: The as-tested cooldown phase of the integrated OTIS test in Chamber A. Slide 9 shows the pre-test prediction of 33 days. A NASA release reprinted by Cold Facts (snapshot 0dab665426a3c162) gives 'about 30 days', after about a week of pump-down. The cited NASA release (792aca5ae634ed68) says only 'a few weeks'.

No source states a time to cool the NTF from ambient to cryogenic-nitrogen operating temperature. The NTF operations simulation memo NTRS 19950025796 (snapshot ff7938cc94f4864e) gives only a maximum cooldown rate (-72 F/hr) and LN2 flow rates. A time could be calculated from these, but it would not be a sourced value. The NTF cooldown also depends on the chosen test temperature. NTRS 19810020601 (48df9108c6ab7a35) gives no cooldown time.

Neither the SMiRF facility page (ab422a7f121203bc), the LAD outflow report NTRS 20140010818 (79555cc5d9789126) nor the Creek Road complex page (1ac14c4716f1b252) gives a chamber or tank chilldown time to 20.3 K.
